h1: Studying distilling and the qualifications that count
title: Distilling Qualifications That Count | Craft Beer School
desc: A guide to distilling qualifications for people in India: degrees, IBD exams, alcohol technology courses and short practical courses.
teaser: There is no single licence to become a distiller. There are qualifications employers recognise and some that matter less.
standfirst: People who want to work in distilling ask the same question: which qualification will get me hired? The honest answer depends on where you start and what role you want. Here is how the main options compare for someone in India.
sections: Start with what employers actually want

Distilleries hire people who can run a process safely, understand what they are measuring and keep accurate records. A qualification helps prove that. It does not replace plant experience. Most hiring managers look for a relevant science or engineering foundation, some proof of distilling knowledge and any hands-on time in a plant or lab.

So the right qualification is the one that fills your specific gap. A chemical engineer needs distilling context. A career changer from another field may need the science first.

Many Indian distillery professionals hold degrees in chemical engineering, chemistry, microbiology, biotechnology or food technology. These cover the underlying science: heat and mass transfer for stills, microbiology for fermentation, analytical chemistry for the lab.

Specialist degrees in brewing and distilling exist abroad. Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh is well known for its brewing and distilling programmes. They are excellent but a large commitment of time and money. Most people in India start with a general science degree and add distilling knowledge on top.

Many Indian distilleries operate alongside sugar mills and use molasses. Sugar technology institutes such as the Vasantdada Sugar Institute in Pune and the National Sugar Institute in Kanpur offer courses in alcohol technology that reflect this industry. Graduates of these courses often join large molasses and grain distilleries in production and quality roles.

These courses focus on industrial ethanol and neutral spirit production. For malt whisky or gin, extra study of pot still distillation, cuts and maturation is usually needed. Check each institute's current course list, as programmes change.

The Institute of Brewing and Distilling (IBD) offers internationally recognised exams. The General Certificate in Distilling is an entry-level qualification covering the whole process. The Diploma in Distilling goes deeper in modules. The Master Distiller qualification sits at the top and is designed for experienced professionals.

IBD exams are self-study with written examinations, so they suit people already working who want to formalise their knowledge. Our guide to IBD distilling qualifications explains each level in more detail.

Short courses fill a different need. They give career changers, brewers and new hires a working grasp of the whole process in weeks rather than years. A good short course covers mashing and fermentation, pot and column distillation, cut points, measuring strength in litres of absolute alcohol plus cask maturation.

They do not replace a degree or an IBD exam, but they make both easier to tackle and make interviews go better. They also suit people planning a craft distillery who need to understand what their distiller will be doing.

Not every course is equal. Before paying for any qualification, ask a few questions. Who teaches it? Have they run a distillery or a distillery lab? Does it cover the full process, from raw material to cask, or only one part? Are there assignments and assessment, or only lectures? Is there a recognised certificate at the end? Can you ask questions live?

Also check whether the course matches your target. A course built around industrial neutral spirit will not teach much about pot still cuts for malt whisky. A gin course will not cover maturation in depth. Matching the course to the role you want saves time and money. Ask past students what they did next, if the provider can put you in touch.

Price matters too, but compare it with the time saved. A course that gets you ready for a trainee interview a year sooner is often worth more than a cheaper one that stays theoretical.

Whatever qualification you hold, time on a plant matters most. Lab internships, shift operator roles and trainee positions all count. Many Indian distilleries run continuously, so entry roles often involve shifts. A year spent reading fermentation curves and recording still strengths teaches what no exam can.

Combine study with practice where you can. Someone working on a plant while studying for the IBD General Certificate is far more employable than someone with either alone.

Write down your current background, the role you want and the gap between them. Then pick the shortest route that closes that gap. Read our guide to becoming a distiller in India for the full career picture.
faqs: It depends on your background. A science degree plus an IBD exam or a practical course suits most people. Plant experience matters most.
Are IBD exams recognised in India?
IBD qualifications are recognised internationally. Indian employers also value local alcohol technology courses and plant experience.
Yes. Short courses and IBD self-study can be done online. Hands-on plant time is still needed.
